title: Intrinsic Vectorial Gradiometry via Quantum Control of a Spin-based Sensor
authors: Jaime García Oliván, Pablo Acedo, Oliver T. Whaites, Jorge Casanova
abstract: Gradiometry provides a versatile alternative to passive environmental shielding in quasi-static magnetometry, effectively suppressing background noise through differential signal extraction. Nevertheless, traditional implementations rely on multi-sensor architectures restricted to spatial gradients, where subtracting signals from independent detectors involves imperfect suppression of common-mode noise and artifacts, limiting their sensitivity. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a quantum control sequence that enables intrinsic temporal and spatial vectorial gradiometry of magnetic fields using a single quantum sensor. Our method provides direct access to first and higher-order derivatives of the magnetic field and extended applicability via auxiliary nuclear spin memory. We showcase this protocol on an ensemble of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond and combine it with mechanical control to realize high-precision differential sensing. Through detailed numerical simulations, we demonstrate the performance of our scheme in two critical DC magnetometry applications: (i) vector magnetic anomaly detection and (ii) non-invasive gradiometry of neuronal action potentials.
summary: This paper introduces a novel quantum control protocol enabling intrinsic vectorial gradiometry of magnetic fields using a single quantum sensor, such as NV centers in diamond. By manipulating spin evolution through controlled pulse sequences, the method suppresses common-mode noise and provides direct access to magnetic field derivatives. This breakthrough has demonstrated potential for high-precision applications like detecting magnetic anomalies and mapping neuronal activity.
main_problem: To overcome the limitations of traditional multi-sensor gradiometry by achieving intrinsic temporal and spatial vectorial gradiometry using a single quantum sensor.
main_result: The proposed quantum control sequence allows for direct measurement of the first and higher-order derivatives of magnetic fields using only one sensor, which can be applied to detect magnetic anomalies or map neuronal action potentials.
method: The method employs a quantum control sequence involving initialization, signal evolution, and readout stages, which can be repeated or modified to measure field differences ($\delta b_i$) or higher-order derivatives ($\langle\sigma_zangle^{(n)}$).
model_or_system: The physical platform is a quantum sensor, specifically Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, which is interrogated using tailored pulse sequences. The theory generalizes the measurement to any pair of electron and nuclear spin qubits.
key_observables: The measured expectation value $\langle\sigma_zangle$, which is proportional to the magnetic field difference ($\delta b_i$) or the $n$-th derivative of the field.
important_parameters: The measurement is limited by the sensor dephasing time ($T_2$), but can be extended to the coherence time ($T_2$) or even the nuclear relaxation time ($T_1$) using memory techniques.
main_assumptions: The initial theoretical derivations assume small accumulated phases ($	ilde{\phi}_1$ small) for the gradient reconstruction, although AC sensing techniques allow for higher frequency measurements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the gradiometric sensing scheme, detailing the multi-stage sequence for measuring field differences, and show circuit diagrams for memory-assisted pulse sequences for intrinsic temporal gradiometry.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first establishing the general quantum control sequence for gradiometry, then extending this to higher-order derivatives, and finally demonstrating the applicability of the protocol to both DC anomaly detection and high-frequency AC sensing via mechanical oscillation.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it develops advanced quantum sensing protocols that leverage quantum coherence and memory effects to achieve superior noise suppression and higher-order field measurements, pushing the boundaries of quantum metrology.

Our protocol comprises an initialization and a readout step, and a measurement sequence (in green, red and blue, respectively), sequentially repeated N times. Our sequence allows to measure the magnetic field difference between two points separated by a time ∆t.
